About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Sociology Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Sociology Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Sociology Years 11–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Sociology Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Sociology, students are taught about the structure of societies and how they
  change, and key concepts such as culture, socialisation, and social stratification.
  Students are taught how to critically examine theories of human behaviour in
  social groups, including analysis of social structures and social institutions, group
  dynamics, and systems of organisation that influence societal behaviour and
  development.

Students are taught core sociological concepts, theories and frameworks that explain
social structures and social institutions, social patterns and social relationships. They
study how theories of human social behaviour have developed over time and the
foundations of sociological research.

Sociology provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse social
issues, social groups, social institutions and patterns and processes in both
contemporary and theoretical contexts. Students apply sociological concepts,
theoretical perspectives, ethical research practices and evidence to investigate social
relationships, influences and inequalities, using sociological reasoning to explain
social behaviour, evaluate competing explanations and examine how power operates
within and between societies.

As students progress through Years 11–13, they are taught to examine critically
theories of human behaviour in social groups, developing the capability to interpret
and analyse social structures and social institutions. This enables them to develop
informed analysis of local, national and global phenomenon.

  Sociology leads to pathways in sociology and related disciplines, such as social
  policy, education, criminology, politics, and media.

Responsible use of artificial intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative
processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues
relating to ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking,
source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-
making. Responsible AI use emphasises the importance of exercising independent
judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent
about AI use, considering diverse perspectives, and developing independent thinking.
